title: STM32: SPI.read(n) fails if n > 1 (regression)
body: I am driving two EEPROM chips over hard SPI at 5 MHz on a Pyboard D SF6W fitted to a DIP28 adaptor. A single-byte read returns the correct value, but a multi-byte read returns a bytes object of the correct length filled with zeros. SoftSPI works, and the same hardware and driver worked with MicroPython v1.18 on a Pyboard D SF2W. A logic-analyser trace shows the EEPROM transmitting the correct MISO data during the failed read, with the clock and chip-select signals looking correct. The traces are very short. Looking at the STM32 SPI code, it appears that multi-byte transfers use DMA while single-byte transfers do not.

symptoms_visible: On the Pyboard D SF6W, spi.read(1) returns the EEPROM byte correctly, but spi.read(n) for n greater than one returns the requested number of zero bytes.
SoftSPI reads the EEPROM correctly, and the logic analyser shows the EEPROM putting the expected data on MISO during the failed hard-SPI read.
N0.label: N0 hard-SPI multi-byte read regression reported

symptoms_visible: The EEPROM still returns zeros for multi-byte hard-SPI reads on current firmware, even though the same test passes on v1.18.
Simple loopback, tied-level, and externally toggled MISO tests do not consistently reproduce what happens with the EEPROM.
N1.label: N1 regression range and hardware configuration collected

symptoms_visible: The EEPROM driver passes with hard SPI when each multi-byte read is replaced by write_readinto using separate write and read buffers.
The regular spi.read call still returns zeros for the same EEPROM data.
N2.label: N2 same-buffer dependency isolated

symptoms_visible: The normal release build can return transmitted fill bytes or zeros instead of all the incoming bytes, with the affected prefix varying between attempts and read lengths.
A test build that compiles the STM32F7 DMA driver with different optimisation passes the full EEPROM test.
N3.label: N3 optimisation-sensitive DMA behaviour measured

symptoms_visible: The branch provided for the final fix reads the EEPROM correctly on my affected Pyboard D, and another affected board also passes its SPI test.
N4.label: N4 final fix verified on test branch

symptoms_visible: On a build containing the final fix, multi-byte hard-SPI reads return the EEPROM data correctly and the full EEPROM test passes.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Can you test older firmware builds and narrow down when the failure first appeared?
What is the newest working release and the earliest failing release?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested the pre-built firmware from the website. v1.18 is the most recent version that passes; v1.19.1 and later fail, so it appeared between January and June 2022.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same EEPROM test also fails on v1.18 and on every older build I tried.
The last working build is a late v1.18 development build rather than the v1.18 release, but v1.19.1 still fails.

question_patterns: Which hardware SPI peripheral are you using?
Does this occur on SPI(1), SPI(2), or more than one peripheral?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I am using SPI(2), which is the only hardware SPI port available on my DIP28 adaptor and the one used by my PCB.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce it with MISO tied high or low, with MOSI looped to MISO, or with an external signal source?
Could you try a minimal electrical reproducer without the EEPROM?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Tying MISO to a level did not demonstrate the EEPROM failure. Linking MOSI and MISO also passed, and a JK flip-flop toggling MISO returned the expected 0x55 bytes. The EEPROM rig still failed after I plugged the same board back into it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every tied-low and loopback test fails in exactly the same deterministic way as the EEPROM.

question_patterns: After reproducing the failure, can you print the SPI pin configurations and compare them with the working firmware?
Are Y6, Y7, and Y8 still configured for the expected SPI2 alternate function?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. On both v1.18 and v1.22.1, Y6, Y7, and Y8 report the expected SPI2 alternate functions. The logic-analyser chip-select trace also behaves the same for single-byte and multi-byte transfers apart from the additional clocks.

edges.comment: Messages c2-c8 from the original reporter: firmware range, SPI(2) configuration, pin inspection, and unsuccessful attempts to reproduce the EEPROM behaviour with simpler wiring.

question_patterns: Can you inspect how spi.read passes its transmit and receive buffer arguments and tell me what the code does?
In the spi.read implementation, do the transmit and receive arguments point to one object or to different objects?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine SPI implementation fills one buffer and passes that same buffer as both the transmit and receive address for spi.read.

question_patterns: Please replace the failing multi-byte reads with write_readinto using different write and read buffers. Does the EEPROM test then work?
Can you compare write_readinto with identical buffers against write_readinto with separate buffers?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I replaced the multi-byte reads with spi.write_readinto using different buffers, and the EEPROM driver now works with hard SPI on STM32 running the latest firmware.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Using separate transmit and receive buffers makes no difference; the received buffer is still filled with zeros.
Separate buffers work for the EEPROM test, but I had to allocate them once outside the read loop.

edges.comment: Messages c12-c18: participant2 identified that spi.read uses one buffer for both directions, and the original reporter confirmed that separate write_readinto buffers make the full driver work. These affected-user contributions are folded into one simulated user side.

question_patterns: Can you rebuild the STM32F7 firmware with different compiler optimisation for the DMA HAL source and report the raw result?
Does rebuilding the DMA driver with -O2 instead of the size optimisation change the SPI read behaviour?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Recompiling the STM32F7 DMA driver with -O2 makes the SPI test work. A DEBUG build and builds using -O1 or -O2 also work here, while the size-optimised build exhibits the failure.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The failure is identical with DEBUG, -O1, -O2, and the normal size-optimised build.
Only -O2 works; the DEBUG and -O1 builds still fail intermittently.

question_patterns: Can you build the candidate optimisation-workaround branch and run the full EEPROM test?
Please test the proposed build on the original EEPROM board rather than only with loopback wiring.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I built the candidate branch and the EEPROM board passed the full test, which is quite rigorous.

question_patterns: Does the problem repeat on consecutive calls and on longer reads?
What raw data do repeated short and long reads return?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It can occur on repeated calls and at all tested lengths. With longer reads, the affected number of bytes varies: some calls return all the transmitted 0x55 fill bytes, while others return a prefix of 0x55 followed by the incoming zero bytes.

edges.comment: Messages c21-c38: participant2's affected SF6/SF2 systems supplied the optimisation, repeated-read, length, and timing results; the original reporter tested the candidate branch on the EEPROM board. These affected systems are folded into the simulated user side. The optimisation result is raw evidence and a workaround, not the final root-cause conclusion.

question_patterns: Please test this branch on an affected board and report what the SPI read returns.
Can you rerun the original EEPROM or flash test using the newly provided branch?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The branch works for me: the original EEPROM test now passes. It also works in the other affected board's test.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The branch still returns zeros from the EEPROM on both affected boards.

edges.comment: Messages c39-c42: participant3 requested testing of the final root-cause branch; participant2 and the original reporter independently confirmed that it works. Both affected-user confirmations are folded into one simulated user side. This is pre-landing candidate verification, so it remains a measurement edge.

solution.intent: Apply the final STM32F7 DMA/cache-coherency fix that prevents Cortex-M7 speculative cache accesses from leaving a shared SPI receive buffer with stale transmit data; retain separate buffers or compiler-optimisation changes only as temporary workarounds.
solution.concrete_example: Use a build containing the final STM32 DMA/cache-handling correction linked from the issue. The earlier write_readinto-with-separate-buffers change and compiling the DMA HAL with -O2 avoid the symptom, but the permanent fix is to make DMA receive-buffer handling safe against Cortex-M7 speculative cache linefills.
solution.inference_hint: The affected users supplied the same-buffer test, optimisation sensitivity, variable read results, and successful branch tests. The final conclusion that rare Cortex-M7 speculative cache linefills explain the optimisation-sensitive stale transmit data is maintainer analysis from c39-c40, not a conclusion the reporter produced from the measurements.

edges.comment: Final accepted diagnosis from c39-c42: the linked root-cause fix addresses Cortex-M7 speculative memory/cache behaviour around STM32 DMA. The final branch was verified by both affected testers before the issue was treated as complete.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as an STM32F7 DMA/cache-coherency problem involving Cortex-M7 speculative cache accesses, not an EEPROM, PCB, pin-mux, chip-select, or signal-integrity fault.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: the EEPROM transmits correct MISO data, spi.read uses one buffer for transmit and receive, separate write/read buffers work, and compiler optimisation changes alter the failure.

Must not present separate write_readinto buffers or compiling the DMA HAL with different optimisation as the permanent fix; they are demonstrated workarounds that helped isolate the cache-sensitive DMA problem.

Must not reject the firmware diagnosis merely because tied-level, loopback, or externally toggled MISO tests sometimes pass; those simplified tests were shown not to reproduce the EEPROM behaviour reliably.
Must ask the affected user to verify a build containing the final DMA/cache fix and treat the issue as resolved only after the original EEPROM test passes.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly experienced MicroPython hardware user and driver author; comfortable building firmware, reading C source, using logic analysers and oscilloscopes, wiring digital test circuits, and running controlled regression tests, while being candid about uncertainty in low-level firmware internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, methodical, and cooperative. Reports exact firmware versions, code, wiring, and raw observations; actively challenges explanations that conflict with measurements without overstating conclusions.
